newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori heads home from Dominican trip.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori heads home from Dominican trip.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori was due to head home early on Monday from the Dominican Republic, where he discussed asylum for Peru's Marxist rebels holding 72 men hostage.
The government and the rebels were to hold fresh talks in Lima later on Monday, aimed at finding a bloodless solution to the 76-day-old crisis.

During a 3-1/2 hour meeting on Sunday with Dominican President Leonel Fernandez, the Peruvian leader floated the idea of possible refuge there for the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary (MRTA) hostage-takers, according to a Dominican government source.
"We are discussing that possibility but there is nothing concrete yet," the source said.
But Fujimori, who flew to Santo Domingo on Sunday for a lightning visit, said the rebels would more likely be given refuge in a third country if there is a deal to peacefully end the crisis.
In a statement issued after the meeting, Fernandez's office said only that the presidents had touched on the hostage crisis.
"President Fujimori gave a brief explanation of the current situation of the talks between the Peruvian government negotiator and the representatives of the MRTA," the statement read.
It added that Fernandez had told Fujimori of the Dominican experience in similar cases.
Fujimori said in a television interview broadcast Sunday in Peru that the Dominican Republic would not be a likely destination for the rebels.
"I don't think the Dominican Republic will be acceptable to them (rebels) as a destination," Fujimori said.
"It's possible that in a third country at some moment it may be necessary and so we're talking about that in an informal way," he added.
He would not reveal the names of countries Peru has approached as possible refuges for the 20-odd rebels who stormed the Japanese ambassador's home on Dec.17.

Fujimori has repeatedly ruled out considering the main MRTA demand -- the release of 400 jailed comrades -- but has indicated he might make other concessions. He has always left the way open to asylum for the rebels.

News reports have said that Cuba, Nicaragua or Eastern Europe could be potential places of asylum in a deal to end Latin America's longest hostage siege. Fujimori said he has not spoken to Cuba's President Fidel Castro about asylum for the Havana-inspired rebels.

Fujimori's trip to the Dominican Republic was his second visit to the Caribbean nation in less than a month, after he met Fernandez during a surprise four-hour stopover at Santo Domingo airport on Feb. 5.
Peruvian government negotiator Domingo Palermo was due to meet the rebels for an eighth time in a Red Cross safehouse near the occupied Japanese ambassador's residence later on Monday.

Officials left the seventh round of talks last Thursday in a relatively upbeat mood, and Fujimori spoke of a "rapprochement" between the two sides. But the rebels sent other signals on Saturday, unfurling defiant new banners promising no surrender.

Late on Sunday, witnesses noted an increased police presence at the siege site in the leafy middle-class district of San Isidro. Police on duty around the fortified compound said the increased number of officers was in response to a security inspection being carried out by senior officers.
The heavily armed squad of mainly teenage MRTA rebels originally took hundreds of hostages when they stormed a cocktail party at the ambassador's residence on Dec. 17.
They freed most captives in the first few weeks of the crisis, but still hold two of Fujimori's relatives, the envoys of Japan and Bolivia, and two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
